Superconductivity and charge-density-wave in the Holstein model on the Penrose Lattice

Lu Liu School of Physics, Beijing Institute of Technology, Beijing 100081, China    Zi-Xiang Li zixiangli@iphy.ac.cn Beijing National Laboratory for Condensed Matter Physics, Institute of Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, China University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100049, China    Fan Yang yangfan_blg@bit.edu.cn School of Physics, Beijing Institute of Technology, Beijing 100081, China
Abstract

The exotic quantum states emerging in the quasicrystal (QC) have attracted extensive interest because of various properties absent in the crystal. In this paper, we systematically study the Holstein model at half filling on a prototypical structure of QC, namely rhombic Penrose lattice, aiming at investigating the superconductivity (SC) and other intertwined ordering arising from the interplay between quasiperiodicity and electron-phonon (e-ph) interaction. Through unbiased sign-problem-free determinant quantum Monte Carlo simulations, we reveal the salient features of the ground-state phase diagram. Distinct from the results on bipartite periodic lattices at half filling, SC is dominant in a large parameter regime on the Penrose lattice. When e-ph coupling is sufficiently strong, charge-density-wave order appears and strongly suppresses the SC. The strongest SC emerges at intermediate e-ph coupling strength and pronounced pairing fluctuation exists above the SC transition temperature. The strong pairing originates from the cooperative effects of unique lattice structure and macroscopically degenerate confined states at Fermi energy which uniquely exist on the Penrose lattice. Moreover, we demonstrate the forbidden ladders substantially suppress the phase coherence of SC. Our unbiased numerical results suggest that Penrose lattice is a potential platform to realize strong SC pairing, providing a promising avenue to searching for relatively high-Tcsubscript𝑇𝑐T_{c} SC dominantly induced by e-ph coupling.

Introduction— The discovery of quasicrystal (QC) sch1 has attracted enduring attention and spurred exciting experimental and theoretical progresses for several decades. QCs possess self-similarity and long-range orientational order but lack transnational symmetry. Moreover, QCs exhibit rotational symmetries such as five-folded or eight-folded ones that are forbidden in conventional crystals. Such special structure results in many exotic physical properties distinct from those of crystals, which includes novel electronic states inayoshi ; rmpjagannathan ; moon ; socolar-fujiwara ; roberts2020 ; sakai ; hauck ; sakai2022 ; sakai2022-2 ; sakai2022-3 ; lesser2022 ; keskiner2022 ; nagai ; sakai2023 ; jagannathan2023 ; jagannathan2023-2 ; ciardi2023 ; keskiner ; sponza2024 ; hecker2024 ; weiren ; kim2024 ; hori2024 ; crosse2021 ; jummojeon2022 , unique topological phase bandres2016 ; kraus ; huang2018 ; longhi2019 ; peng2021 ; jeon2022 ; cwang2022 ; bhola2022 ; ghadimi2023 ; rchen2023 ; yang2024 ; madsen ; flicker ; rchen2023 ; junmojeon2024 . Increasingly more attention has been paid to the correlated systems on QC jagannathan2007 ; jagannathan2012 ; wessel2003 ; shaginyan2013 ; thiem2015 ; andrade2015 ; otsuki2016 ; koga2017 ; miyazaki2020 ; koga2021 ; koga2022 ; ghosh2023 ; ionue ; khansili since the discovery of quantum critical behavior in Au-Al-Yb QC qc-exp . Particularly, as a typical macroscopic quantum phenomenon, the superconductivity (SC) has been observed experimentally in a Al-Zn-Mg QC sc-exp , along with the earlier results on ternary QCs wong1987 ; wagner1988 and crystalline approximates deguchi2015 , stimulating extensive experiment and theoretical investigation to understand the intriguing properties of SC on the QC grai ; grai2 ; uri2023 ; sakai2017 ; jhou2018 ; autti2018 ; araujo1 ; sakai2019 ; takemori ; nagai2020 ; shiino2021 ; khosravian2021 ; yubo2022 ; fukushima2023 ; fukushima2023-2 ; ybliu2023 ; yecao ; hori2024-1 ; sandberg2024 ; kobialka2024 ; ghadimi ; saito2020 ; ghadimi2021 ; hori2024-2 ; cunyuanjiang . Recently a convincing observation of superconductivity in the Ta-Te QC was reported terashima2024 ; tokumoto2024 , which further emphasizes the importance of SC research on QC.

The SC observed in both Al-Zn-Mg and Ta-Te QCs originate from the electron-phonon (e-ph) interaction. The e-ph interaction is of fundamental importance in triggering the formation of Cooper pairs in the most conventional superconductors, as proposed in the celebrated Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer theory. In the context of e-ph interaction, previous studies of the SC on the QC are focused on the simplified attractive Hubbard model with the treatment of mean-field calculation araujo1 ; sakai2017 ; sakai2019 ; nagai2020 ; takemori ; yubo2022 . The attractive Hubbard model, as an effective interacting model accounting for the e-ph coupling, does not incorporate the retardation effect in the electronic interaction mediated by phonon fields, which affects the superconducting transition temperature (Tcsubscript𝑇𝑐T_{c}) and the emergence of other ordering tendencies. Particularly, in the regime of small phonon frequency relevant to most realistic materials, the other electronic instabilities arises. For instance, charge-density-wave (CDW) order or bipolaron are driven by the e-ph coupling, competing with the SC and tremendously suppressing the superconducting Tcsubscript𝑇𝑐T_{c} kivelson2018 ; lee2019 ; AlexandreReview . The competition between the SC and other electronic instabilities in the e-ph coupling dominated systems of QC is not captured by previous theoretical studies. Moreover, the superconducting fluctuation beyond mean-field calculation generally influences the phase coherence of pairingkivelson1995 . The systematical illustration of the interplay between pairing fluctuation and the special electronic structure on the Penrose lattice such as macroscopically degenerate and confined states, and the cooperative effects of them on the SC and other competing orders are still lacking but essential. Hence, the investigation on the e-ph interaction on QC through an approximation-free theoretical approach that takes all these crucial ingredients into accounts is immensely desired, which will definitely lead a great leap to systematically fathoming the phonon mediated SC and the competition with other dominant instabilities such as CDW on QC.

To address this critical issue, we perform numerically-exact determinant quantum Monte-Carlo (DQMC) simulation on the Holstein e-ph coupling model on a representative QC, namely Penrose lattice pen-til . The Holstein model holstein is a prototypical microscopic model characterizing the e-ph coupling, which has been extensively studied in the periodic-crystal systems. Here, for the first time we systematically investigate the finite-temperature properties of the model on QC, particularly focusing on the SC and CDW order triggered by the e-ph interaction, through unbiased DQMC approach without involving any uncontrolled approximation. We focus on the simulation at half filling. The DQMC results reveal the salient feature of phase diagram with varying e-ph interaction strength. Remarkably, SC is the dominant ordering in the presence of weak e-ph interaction. The SC persists up to an intermediate coupling regime, coexisting with CDW order. With the enhancement of CDW order, SC is suppressed by the strong e-ph interaction. The emergence of SC-CDW coexistence in a large coupling regime of e-ph interaction on the half-filled Penrose lattice is distinct from the results of Holstein model on the half-filled bipartite periodic-crystal systems, in which CDW orders are dominant over SC. The difference might originates from the special electronic structures on QC, which provides a promising route to enhancing SC mediated by e-ph interaction. When the e-ph coupling is strong enough, it will be CDW order in the ground state.

Model and method— The Penrose lattice is a prototypical structure of a two-dimensional QC. It can be constructed from two types of rhombuses, which is shown in Fig.1(a). The Penrose lattice has a set of vertices with coordination number z𝑧z ranging from 333 to 777. The average coordination number is exactly 444. The Penrose tiling can also be created by the inflation-deflation process, manifesting self-similarity of the lattice. One important feature of the Penrose lattice is the macroscopically degenerate single-particle states. These states are dubbed as confined states and their wave functions are strictly confined in a finite region in the lattice kohmoto ; arai . As depicted in Fig. 1(a), each confined state is confined in a colored structure unit dubbed as cluster, and the clusters are separated by stripe regions (called forbidden ladders arai ; koga2017 ), indicated by the white region in Fig. 1(a) (see Supplementary Information (SI) for details). More intriguingly, the energies of the macroscopically degenerate confined states are exactly zero, rendering the infinite density of state at E=0𝐸0E=0, as shown in Fig. 1(b). In the following, we scrutinize the interplay between these unique electronic structures and e-ph interaction on the Penrose lattice.

To numerically study the effect of e-ph interaction, we consider a typical e-ph model, termed as Holstein model, with the Hamiltonian reading:

With increasing phonon frequency from Ω=1Ω1\Omega=1 to Ω=4Ω4\Omega=4, the SC is enhanced as evidenced by the increase of the superconducting susceptibility. For Ω=4Ω4\Omega=4, the SC is enhanced with increasing e-ph coupling strength in a large parameter regime of g𝑔g, being strongest at g=6𝑔6g=6. The power-law fit of the inverse of susceptibility confirm the existence of long-range order of SC at ground state for g≤6𝑔6g\leq 6. For Ω=4Ω4\Omega=4, the 1/χSC1subscript𝜒SC1/\chi_{\rm SC} displays the feature of divergence at a relatively high temperature. For instance, for g=6𝑔6g=6, the fitting of 1/χSC1subscript𝜒SC1/\chi_{\rm SC} showcases the divergence of susceptibility occurring at T≃0.06similar-to-or-equals𝑇0.06T\simeq 0.06, implying the possibility of relatively high Tcsubscript𝑇𝑐T_{c} of SC. As e-ph coupling is further increased, the SC is suppressed as revealed by the decrease of χSCsubscript𝜒SC\chi_{\rm SC}. We emphasize that the fitting results of the Tcsubscript𝑇𝑐T_{c} are not the real transition temperature in the thermodynamic limit, as there are finite size effect. We present the finite size effect in SI and expect the real Tcsubscript𝑇𝑐T_{c} little larger than the fitting results.

To further investigate the properties of SC on Penrose lattice, we evaluate local density of state (LDOS) through computing single-particle time-dependent Greens’ function in DQMC (see the SI for details). LDOS is a crucial observable measurable in the experiment of scanning tunnelling microscope, revealing the spectral properties in various phases. We choose the parameters in the regime where the SC is strong by fixing Ω=4Ω4\Omega=4 and g=4.0𝑔4.0g=4.0, and calculate LDOS at two typical positions on the Penrose lattice. At sufficiently low temperature, such as T=1/15𝑇115T=1/15, the spectral gap is fully opened and two sharp coherence peaks with particle-hole symmetry appear, suggesting the emergence of SC. The sizes of gap are approximately same in center of cluster and in the forbidden ladder, as depicted in Fig. 3 (a) and (b), while the coherence peaks are slightly broader in the forbidden ladder compared with the result of cluster center. With increasing temperature for T≥1/10𝑇110T\geq 1/10, the peaks evidently broaden but remain well-defined in a large temperature regime. The feature of (pseudo) gap revealed by the suppression of spectral function at Fermi energy persists up to a significantly higher temperature than SC Tcsubscript𝑇𝑐T_{c}. Since the spectral peaks are particle-hole symmetric, strong SC fluctuation is a possible origin of the (pseudo) gaps above Tcsubscript𝑇𝑐T_{c}. The strong pairing between electrons is robust in a temperature regime above Tcsubscript𝑇𝑐T_{c}, in which the phase coherence is destroyed by the thermal fluctuation of SC pairing. Consequently, our results indicate the strong SC pairing is formed on the Penrose lattice induced by e-ph coupling, rendering the SC fluctuation and spectral gaps above Tcsubscript𝑇𝑐T_{c}.

Charge-density-wave order: In addition to the SC, CDW order is usually another prevalent instability triggered by e-ph interaction, particularly in the strong coupling regime. For half filling Holstein model on bipartite lattice , the CDW order is always dominant over SC at finite phonon frequency. For example, the dominant instability is CDW order with momentum (π,π)𝜋𝜋(\pi,\pi) on square lattice, which is attributed to the Fermi-surface nesting (FSN) in the weakly coupling regime and the formation of bipolaron in the presence of strong e-ph interaction. On the Penrose lattice, despite that the lattice momentum is not a good quantum number due to the lack of transnational symmetry, the CDW order parameter is well defined as the difference of particle number on two sublattices because Penrose lattice is bipartite. The CDW order parameter and the associated structure factor are explicitly expressed as:

To detect the CDW order, we calculate the CDW structure factor SCDWsubscript𝑆CDWS_{\rm CDW} defined in Eq.(4). Fig. 4 (a) and (b) present the results of Ω=1Ω1\Omega=1 and Ω=4Ω4\Omega=4, respectively. The results reveal that when g𝑔g is small, SCDWsubscript𝑆CDWS_{\rm CDW} changes little as the temperature decreases, implying the absence of CDW long-range order at the ground state. However, when e-ph coupling is strong, the CDW order is significantly enhanced. At Ω=1Ω1\Omega=1, when g≥1.0𝑔1.0g\geq 1.0, SCDWsubscript𝑆CDWS_{\rm CDW} increases rapidly with lowering temperature. The divergent behavior suggests the emergence of CDW long-range order at sufficiently low temperature for g≥1.0𝑔1.0g\geq 1.0. With the enhancement of CDW order, the SC is substantially suppressed. Nevertheless, the SC and CDW coexist at several values of g𝑔g in the intermediate coupling regime such as g=1.0𝑔1.0g=1.0. The increase of phonon frequency weaken the CDW order and enhance the SC. At Ω=4Ω4\Omega=4, the CDW order is short-range in a larger coupling regime, namely g≤4.0𝑔4.0g\leq 4.0, compared with the results for Ω=1Ω1\Omega=1. When g≥4.0𝑔4.0g\geq 4.0, SCDWsubscript𝑆CDWS_{\rm CDW} also increases significantly and exhibits the divergent behavior with lowering temperature, suggesting the existence of long-range ordering at ground state. For Ω=4Ω4\Omega=4, the coexistence of the SC and CDW long-range order is present in a larger coupling regime, namely 4.0≥g≥6.04.0𝑔6.04.0\geq g\geq 6.0, compared with the situation for Ω=1.0Ω1.0\Omega=1.0.

Enhancement of pairing on Penrose lattice: Now we arrive at the ground-state phase diagram of the half filling Holstein model on the Penrose lattice. The ground state is the SC and the superconducting order is enhanced with increasing the value of g𝑔g in the weakly coupling regime. In the presence of strong e-ph coupling, the CDW order is dominant and the SC is suppressed. There is a coexistent regime of the SC and CDW order. With increasing phonon frequency, the parameter regimes of e-ph coupling for the SC phase and coexistent phase of SC and CDW order are notably enlarged. The schematic phase diagram is presented in Fig. 1 (c). Notice that the phase diagram of Holstein model on Penrose lattice is qualitatively different from the ones on bipartite lattice for periodic crystals. For the periodic crystals on bipartite lattice, the band structure either processes Fermi-surface nesting or features Dirac points at the Fermi energy for the half electronic filling number. In the former situation of FSN, the ground state is CDW phase in the whole coupling regime for the finite phonon frequency. For instance the ground state is CDW ordered phase carrying momentum (π,π)𝜋𝜋(\pi,\pi) on square lattice. For the systems featuring Dirac points, typically the Honeycomb-lattice model, the Dirac semi-metal phase is robust against weak e-ph coupling, and the CDW order emerges in the strong e-ph coupling regime. In contrast, the FSN is absent on the Penrose lattice due to the lacking of well-defined lattice momentum, resulting in the absence of CDW long-range ordering at weakly coupling regime. Consequently, even at half filling, the SC is the dominant ordering in a large e-ph coupling strength regime on Penrose lattice.

Additionally, the results of single-particle spectrum and DOS on Penrose lattice, as shown in Fig. 1(b), indicate a pronounced peak of DOS at zero energy. In the celebrated BCS theory for periodic lattice, the SC pairing amplitude increases with the DOS at Fermi energy. Here, for the QC without transnational symmetry, presumably the pairing should also be enhanced by the divergent DOS at zero energy. Moreover, the competing orders arising from the large DOS including density-wave ordering are suppressed on the Penrose lattice. The large pairing gap and possible strong SC fluctuation above Tcsubscript𝑇𝑐T_{c}, as revealed by the spectral results, confirm the formation of strong SC pairing induced by the e-ph coupling on the Penrose lattice.

The effect of forbidden ladders: As aforementioned, on Penrose lattice a large amount of zero-energy states are confined in a region separated by the forbidden ladders, dubbed as confined states, give rise to the divergent DOS at zero energy. Despite that the formation of pairing is enhanced by the confined states, the nature of confinement is expected to suppress the phase coherence of the SC pairing. To characterize such effect, we compute the expectation values of hopping term Ti​j=12(ci†cj+cj†ci))T_{ij}=\frac{1}{2}(c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{j}+c_{j}^{\dagger}c_{i})) and pair correlation Δi​ΔjsubscriptΔ𝑖subscriptΔ𝑗\Delta_{i}\Delta_{j} on each nearest neighbor bond. The results for Ω=1Ω1\Omega=1 and g=1𝑔1g=1 are presented in Fig. 5(a) and (b) (results for another parameters are shown in the SI), which demonstrates the values of Ti​jsubscript𝑇𝑖𝑗T_{ij} and Δi​ΔjsubscriptΔ𝑖subscriptΔ𝑗\Delta_{i}\Delta_{j} are significantly weakened in the forbidden ladder. It suggests the suppression of SC pairing coherence in this region. With increasing e𝑒{\it e}-ph coupling strength, the amplitudes of Ti​jsubscript𝑇𝑖𝑗T_{ij} and Δi​ΔjsubscriptΔ𝑖subscriptΔ𝑗\Delta_{i}\Delta_{j} in the forbidden ladder, as dictated in Fig. 5(c) and (d), increase in the weakly coupling regime and exhibit maximum values in the intermediate coupling regime, in alignment with the results of SC susceptibility shown in Fig. 2. The results suggest that the property of confined states separated by the forbidden ladder is a crucial ingredient affecting the SC in Penrose lattice. The nature of localization for the confined state is suppressed in the presence of intermediate e𝑒{\it e}-ph coupling, resulting in the enhancement of the SC phase coherence.

Discussions and Conclusions: In conclusion, we perform unbiased DQMC simulation to study a representative model of e-ph coupling, namely Holstein model, on the Penrose lattice. We systematically investigate the properties of SC and other competed instabilities such as CDW order, revealing the phase diagram of the model. The SC is dominant in a large regime of coupling strength. When e-ph coupling is strong, the CDW order prevails over the SC, and there exists a coexistent regime of SC and CDW. The strongest SC emerges at the intermediate coupling regime.

Many intriguing properties of SC are triggered by the interplay between quasiperiodicity and electron-phonon interaction, distinguished from the ones on periodic lattice. Owing to the absence of translational symmetry, the density-wave instabilities such as CDW order, which are generically dominant on periodic lattice in the presence of e-ph coupling, are strongly suppressed on the Penrose lattice. Hence, the phase diagram of Holstein model on Penrose lattice at half filling is qualitatively different from the one in half-filled Holstein model on bipartite periodic lattice, in which CDW ordering is dominant and SC is absent. Moreover, the particularly strong pairing is induced by the e-ph coupling on the Penrose lattice, arising from the divergent DOS at zero energy. The strong pairing results in the pronounced SC fluctuation and spectral gap above SC Tcsubscript𝑇𝑐T_{c}. The Penrose lattice is a promising platform to realize relatively high-Tcsubscript𝑇𝑐T_{c} SC dominantly driven by e-ph coupling. Moreover, the forbidden ladder separating different regions of confined states, which uniquely exists on the Penrose lattice, is also a crucial ingredient determining the properties of SC through affecting the phase coherence of pairing.

We also have studied the properties of the uniform spin susceptibilities. We find the susceptibilities do not diverge for any calculated strength of e-ph coupling, indicating finite spin gap and missing magnetic order for the system.

The Hostein model studied here is the simplest one to describe the e-ph coupling, and more sophisticated model such as the SSH model ssh1 ; ssh2 ; ssh4 ; ssh3 ; ssh5 ; ssh6 can also be simulated by the sign-free DQMC approach, albeit with more technical difficulties. The SSH model can capture more features of the lattice vibration in the QC, including the presence of the low-energy phason mode phason1 ; phason2 , and thus it provides a viable platform to study the role of the phason mode in mediating the SC. We leave this topic for the future study.

Methods

Quantum Monte Carlo. We employed the ALF method1 implementation of the auxiliary-field finite-temperature quantum Monte Carlo method. The determined quantum Monte Carlo method about Holstein model is based on method . The imaginary-time discretisation is Δ​τ=0.1Δ𝜏0.1\Delta\tau=0.1. To obtain the results of local density of state, we perform stochastic analytical continuation (SAC) approach to extract the real-frequency results from the imaginary-time single-particle Green’s functionmethod2 . The details of the approach implemented in our simulation are included in the SI.

I Supplementary Information

I.1 Penrose lattices in our simulations

We actually simulate the Penrose lattice for 666 different site number. The site number are N=31,46,76,101,141,201𝑁314676101141201N=31,46,76,101,141,201 respectively. These lattices are shown in Fig. 6.

I.2 Confined states, Clusters and Forbidden ladders

All the confined states can be classified to the six types depicted in Fig. 7 kohmoto ; arai ; koga2017 . Koga defined the domain of each type of confined state by two rules in Ref. koga2017 : the confined state has zero and a finite amplitude alternately along its boundary, and its area is maximized. When we cover the Penrose lattice with the six types of confined state domains, domains may overlap to cover certain larger parts, which are called clusters. We can find these parts are separated by strips, which are a set of unbranched closed loops. These strips, call forbidden ladder, are made of the rhombuses that do not belong to any confined state domains. Thus the confined states exist only on certain cluster. The clusters and forbidden ladders are show in Fig. 1(a) and Fig. 6.

One can easily find that the energies of every type of confined state are all E=0𝐸0E=0. According to the Conway’s theorem, a local pattern must have duplicates that extend throughout the whole lattice conway . As the six types of confined state are all finite-size, their densities are also finite, which leads to the infinite DOS for confined state at E=0𝐸0E=0. One can refer to Refs. arai ; koga2017 to find the quantitative calculation of the number/density of confined states in Penrose lattice.

I.6 The details of Stochastic analytical continuation

In the simulation of determinant quantum Monte-Carlo (DQMC), it is straightforward to compute the imaginary-time single-particle Green’s function Gi​j​(τ)=⟨ci​(0)​cj​(τ)†⟩subscript𝐺𝑖𝑗𝜏delimited-⟨⟩subscript𝑐𝑖0subscript𝑐𝑗superscript𝜏†G_{ij}(\tau)=\left\langle c_{i}(0)c_{j}(\tau)^{\dagger}\right\rangle. In the maintext, we present the results of local density of state (LDOS), which is evaluated from the local imaginary-time Green’s function Gi​i​(τ)=⟨ci​(0)​ci​(τ)†⟩subscript𝐺𝑖𝑖𝜏delimited-⟨⟩subscript𝑐𝑖0subscript𝑐𝑖superscript𝜏†G_{ii}(\tau)=\left\langle c_{i}(0)c_{i}(\tau)^{\dagger}\right\rangle. The real-frequency LDOS is related to the local imaginary-time Green’s function through the formula:

Gi​i​(τ)=∫d​ω2​π​e−τ​ω​ρi​(ω)e−β​ω+1,subscript𝐺𝑖𝑖𝜏𝑑𝜔2𝜋superscript𝑒𝜏𝜔subscript𝜌𝑖𝜔superscript𝑒𝛽𝜔1\displaystyle G_{ii}(\tau)=\int\frac{d\omega}{2\pi}\frac{e^{-\tau\omega}\rho_{i}(\omega)}{e^{-\beta\omega}+1}, (5)

where ρi​(ω)subscript𝜌𝑖𝜔\rho_{i}(\omega) is the LDOS at site i𝑖i and β𝛽\beta is inverse temperature. Extracting ρi​(ω)subscript𝜌𝑖𝜔\rho_{i}(\omega) from Gi​i​(τ)subscript𝐺𝑖𝑖𝜏G_{ii}(\tau) is challenging due to the statistical error of Gi​isubscript𝐺𝑖𝑖G_{ii} outputted from DQMC simulation. To achieve the reliable results of ρi​(ω)subscript𝜌𝑖𝜔\rho_{i}(\omega), we implement the approach of stochastic analytical continuation (SAC), which is a powerful algorithm in the numerical analytical continuation from the imaginary-time Green’s function to the real-frequency observables. The approach of SAC converts the ill-conditioned inversion problem into a Monte-Carlo sampling process. The details of the SAC algorithm is introduced in method2 . In our simulation, we set the frequency range of the LDOS as ω∈[−30,30]𝜔3030\omega\in[-30,30], which is sufficient large to guarantee convergence of the results. The frequency grid is fixed with spacing δ​ω=5×10−3𝛿𝜔5superscript103\delta\omega=5\times 10^{-3}. We run 12 independent Markov chains in the SAC, with each one containing 50000-100000 Monte-Carlo samples depending on the temperature in the DQMC simulation.
